buildUp: Start from the coffee: about 18 g of fine grounds packed into a steel basket with a perforated floor, which needs about 9 bar of water to flow through it in about half a minute.
Something has to make that pressure, so a small vibration pump draws water from a reservoir and pushes it, with a valve to stop the pressure going above about 9 bar at the coffee.
The water must also be hot, so it needs a boiler and an element. Running the boiler above 100 °C under pressure gives steam for milk too, and a pressure switch holds it there.
That boiler water is far too hot for coffee, so brewing water instead passes through a copper heat-exchanger tube inside the boiler and comes out at about 93 °C.
The basket has to be locked under the water at 9 bar and removed easily, so it sits in a handled portafilter that twists into a heavy group head with a rubber gasket.
A cold group would chill each shot, so a loop of pipes keeps hot water circulating through it, and a lever on top starts the pump, opens the water and vents the pressure when you finish.
Last come the comforts: a gauge to show when it's ready, wands for steam and hot water, a drip tray, a cup warmer and a stainless case to hold it all.
firstPrinciples.coreIdea: Grind the coffee very fine and use force to push the water through it. A pump squeezes water at about 9 bar through a tightly packed puck of grounds, so the huge surface area of the fine grind is extracted in 25 to 30 seconds. A pressurised boiler kept well above 100 °C supplies steam, and a tube running through it heats the brewing water to just the right temperature on the way to the coffee.

hardParts.title: Getting the brewing temperature right with one boiler
hardParts.why: The boiler has to be about 123 °C for good steam, but coffee wants about 93 °C. The heat exchanger and thermosiphon cool it to roughly the right range, but water left still in the tube overheats, and how hot a shot comes out depends on how long the machine has been idle. That's why owners learn to do a 'cooling flush', and why fancier machines use two separate boilers.

hardParts.title: Sealing 9 bar in a joint you open twenty times a day
hardParts.why: The portafilter has to hold back about nine times atmospheric pressure, yet come off with a quick twist and survive being banged on a knock box. Two lugs, a slot in the group and a thick rubber gasket do it, but the gasket hardens with heat over time and starts to leak.

hardParts.title: Making water flow evenly through the coffee
hardParts.why: Water always takes the easiest path, so any crack or loose spot in the puck lets it rush through there and leave the rest under-extracted, a fault called channelling. Fine even grinding, careful tamping, a shower screen that spreads the water and a gentle pre-infusion soak all exist to stop it.

principles.explanation: Grinding finer makes the coffee give up its flavour much faster, but it packs the grounds so tightly that only pressure can push water through them in seconds. Flavour dissolves from the surface of each grain, so grinding finer exposes far more surface. But the gaps between fine particles are tiny, so the packed puck resists flow like a wet sponge. Ground as fine as espresso needs, a packed puck would take minutes to drip through by gravity alone.
principles.title: Finer grind, faster flavour, more resistance

principles.explanation: Sealed under steam pressure, boiler water stays liquid until about 123 °C, so one tank can hold water hot enough to make plenty of steam for milk. Water boils when its molecules have enough energy to push back against the pressure above them, so letting steam build up in a sealed boiler, to about 1.2 bar over the air outside, raises the boiling point. That's also why the gauge on the front, which reads pressure, is really a thermometer.
principles.title: Pressure raises the boiling point

principles.explanation: Fresh brewing water runs through a copper tube inside the boiler, borrowing heat from the boiler water through the tube wall without ever mixing with it. A copper tube full of fresh water sitting in 123 °C boiler water warms up quickly, because copper passes heat well and the temperature difference is large. Run it through fast enough and it comes out at about 90 to 96 °C, which is the window where coffee tastes sweet rather than sour or bitter.
principles.title: Heat flows from hot to cold, through a wall

principles.explanation: Because hot water rises, a loop of pipe between the heat exchanger and the group keeps water circulating with no pump, holding the heavy brass group at brewing temperature all day. Warm water is slightly less dense than cool water, so it floats upwards. In the loop, hot water rises from the heat exchanger through one pipe while cooler water sinks back from the group through the other. That slow, steady flow is called a thermosiphon.
principles.title: Hot water rises

firstPrinciples.problem: Get the flavour out of coffee in under half a minute instead of the four minutes a cafetière takes, and make it strong, thick and rich enough to drink in a few sips. Hot water only dissolves coffee slowly, and making the grind finer speeds it up but also packs the grounds so tightly that water can barely get through. On top of that, the same small machine should also make steam for milk, which needs water far hotter than coffee can stand.

questions.answer: The grind is so fine that the packed coffee lets water through only very slowly; gravity alone would take minutes and the coffee would be over-extracted and bitter. It takes about 9 bar of pressure to push the water through in 25 to 30 seconds.
questions.question: Why can't you make espresso just by pouring hot water over finely ground coffee?

questions.answer: In a sealed boiler with steam on top, pressure and temperature are tied together: the hotter the water, the more steam pressure it makes. About 1.2 bar always means about 123 °C, so the pressure reading is effectively a temperature reading.
questions.question: If the gauge only measures pressure, how does it tell you the machine is hot enough?

questions.answer: Water left still in the heat-exchanger tube keeps soaking up heat from the 123 °C boiler around it until it's much hotter than 93 °C. Running a short cooling flush pushes that overheated water out so fresh water, warmed on its way through, reaches the coffee.
questions.question: Why does a heat-exchanger machine often brew too hot if it's been sitting idle?

firstPrinciples.xFactor: The E61 group's real trick isn't its looks; it's that it solved temperature and pressure with plumbing rather than electronics. The thermosiphon keeps four kilos of brass at a steady temperature with no pump, the spring-loaded pre-infusion chamber gently wets the coffee before full pressure arrives, and the three-way valve vents the leftover pressure so the portafilter comes off clean. A design from 1961 with no software at all still makes excellent coffee, which is why so many makers still build it.

name: Espresso Machine
overview:
An espresso machine makes a small, strong coffee by forcing hot water through a tightly packed puck of finely ground coffee. About 18 g of coffee goes into a steel basket, is pressed flat, and locked under the machine in a handled holder called the portafilter. Water at roughly 93 °C is then pushed through it at about 9 bar, nine times the pressure of the air around us, and after 25 to 30 seconds about 36 g of thick, syrupy coffee with a layer of golden crema runs into the cup.

The pressure comes from a small vibration pump that draws cold water from a reservoir in the back. The heat comes from a copper boiler with an electric element inside, kept hot by a pressure switch. In this heat-exchanger design the boiler is kept hotter than brewing temperature, so it has steam on top for frothing milk, and fresh water for coffee is heated on its way through a copper tube that runs through the boiler. A pair of pipes links that tube to the group head in a loop, so hot water circulates on its own and keeps the heavy brass group at the right temperature.

The group head on the front is the famous E61, introduced by Faema in 1961. Lifting its lever switches on the pump and opens valves inside the group; lowering it closes them and vents the leftover pressure into the drip tray, so the portafilter can be taken off straight away. Around all this sits a box of stainless-steel panels, a gauge showing the boiler pressure, and wands for steam and hot water.

parts.description: Slotted steel tray on top where cups sit to warm up from the heat rising off the boiler.

details.didYouKnow: Espresso cups are traditionally thick-walled china precisely so they hold heat; a warm thick cup keeps the shot hot for longer than a thin one.
details.howItWorks: The tray sits on the case top, right above the boiler. Heat from the boiler rises through the case and warms whatever stands on it, so espresso cups are already hot when the coffee hits them. A cold, thick china cup can knock several degrees off a small shot in seconds, which is why baristas keep their cups up here.
keyNumbers: Holds a handful of espresso cups
Takes a good half hour to warm through
details.madeOf: Stainless steel, pressed or cut into a slotted pattern so warm air can come up through it, often with a polished rail round the edge to stop cups sliding off.

parts.name: Cup-warmer tray

parts.description: Stainless lid of the case; it lifts off to fill the reservoir and to reach the boiler.

details.didYouKnow: Many machines have small vents in the case so the inside doesn't cook the electronics; the cup tray doubles as one of them.
details.howItWorks: The top is the lid of the case. On many machines it lifts off, or has a flap at the back, so you can reach in and fill the reservoir. Underneath it is a gap above the boiler where the hottest air collects, which is what warms the cup tray.
keyNumbers: Sits just above the hottest part of the machine
details.madeOf: A sheet of stainless steel about 1 mm thick, folded at the edges for stiffness.

parts.name: Case top

parts.description: Stainless side panel, screwed to the frame; the machine's body is just a box of these.

details.didYouKnow: Polished stainless side panels are a big part of why these machines cost what they do; the shiny boxy look is a deliberate nod to Italian café machines.
details.howItWorks: The side panels carry no load to speak of; they keep fingers away from hot pipes and mains wiring and make the machine look like one solid block. They're held on by a few screws, so a technician can take them off to reach the boiler and pump.
details.madeOf: Polished or brushed stainless steel, chosen because it doesn't rust in a warm, steamy kitchen and wipes clean easily.

parts.name: Left side panel

parts.description: The other side panel; with it off you can see the pump, the boiler and the plumbing.

details.didYouKnow: Most of these machines are put together by hand in small Italian workshops, with each panel fitted and polished by a person rather than a robot.
details.howItWorks: This is the panel you'd take off first to service the machine. Behind it is the plumbing: the pump on the base, the solenoid valve, the pressurestat and the copper pipes running up to the boiler. Inside, the panels get warm but not dangerous; the boiler itself is often wrapped in insulation.
keyNumbers: The inside of the case can reach 50 °C or so
details.madeOf: The same stainless steel sheet as the other side, cut and folded on a press.

parts.name: Right side panel

parts.description: Rear panel with a cut-out for the mains cable; it comes off to reach the reservoir and wiring.

details.didYouKnow: Because the reservoir sits at the back, many owners leave the back panel free of the wall so they can lift the tank out without dragging the machine forward.
details.howItWorks: The back closes the case behind the reservoir and carries the mains socket or cable. On some machines it's shaped to let the reservoir slide out from the back or the top.
keyNumbers: Machine draws up to about 1,400 W
Usually needs 10 cm clear behind for air
details.madeOf: Stainless steel, with a moulded plastic grommet where the mains cable comes through.

parts.name: Back panel

parts.description: Polished front that carries the gauge, the switches and the knobs, with the group head bolted through it.

details.didYouKnow: On many machines the front is the only panel whose look changes between models; the boiler, pump and plumbing behind it are often almost identical across brands.
details.howItWorks: The front panel is the face of the machine: the group head bolts through it, and it carries the pressure gauge, the power switch and the steam and hot-water knobs. Because you stand in front of it all day, it's usually the most polished panel.
keyNumbers: Holds the gauge, switch and two knobs
Carries the 4 kg or so of group head through its mounting
details.madeOf: Polished stainless steel with holes punched for the gauge, switches, valve spindles and the group's mounting.

parts.name: Front panel

parts.description: Steel base plate that the pump, boiler and panels are all bolted to.

details.didYouKnow: A heavy machine is actually useful: locking in and removing the portafilter takes a real twist, and a light machine would slide across the worktop.
details.howItWorks: Everything heavy is bolted to the base: the boiler sits on brackets above it, the pump hangs from rubber mounts on it, and the panels screw to its edges. It also gives the machine its weight and steadiness when you lock in the portafilter with a firm twist.
keyNumbers: Whole machine weighs about 20 to 25 kg
Pump hung on rubber to cut vibration
details.madeOf: Painted or stainless steel plate, folded up at the edges, with captive nuts for the brackets.

parts.name: Base frame

parts.description: Rubber feet under the corners that grip the worktop and soak up the pump's buzz.

details.didYouKnow: A level machine matters more than you'd think: if it tilts, the coffee bed in the basket can form unevenly and water takes the easy path down one side.
details.howItWorks: Four rubber feet hold the base just off the worktop. They grip the surface so the machine doesn't move when you twist the portafilter, and soak up the hum of the vibration pump so it isn't amplified by a hollow worktop.
keyNumbers: Carry 20 kg or more between them
details.madeOf: Rubber or silicone pads, sometimes on screw-adjustable stems so the machine can be levelled.

parts.name: Feet

parts.description: Shallow tray under the group that catches drips and the water vented when the lever is lowered; it slides out to empty.

details.didYouKnow: On café machines the drip tray is plumbed straight into a drain; at home it simply fills up, and forgetting to empty it is the classic way to flood a worktop.
details.howItWorks: The tray sits under the group and the wands to catch drips, spills and the burst of water and wet grounds that the group vents through its drain when you lower the lever. It slides straight out of the front to be emptied.
keyNumbers: Emptied about once a day in normal use
details.madeOf: Stainless steel, pressed into a shallow box with rounded corners so it's easy to clean.

parts.name: Drip tray

parts.description: Slotted cover on the drip tray that the cup stands on.

details.didYouKnow: The gap between the grate and the spouts decides which cups fit; tall glasses for a latte often don't, which is why some trays can be lowered.
details.howItWorks: The grate is the cup rest. Drips fall straight through its slots into the tray below, and the cup sits flat and dry on top, right under the portafilter's spouts.
keyNumbers: Sits roughly 10 cm below the spouts
details.madeOf: Stainless steel, punched or welded into a lattice.

parts.name: Drip tray grate

parts.description: Dial on the front showing the steam pressure in the boiler, usually between 1 and 1.5 bar when it's ready.

details.didYouKnow: Bourdon tube gauges were invented in 1849 and still work with no electricity at all; they're the same kind found on steam locomotives.
details.howItWorks: A curved hollow tube inside the gauge, called a Bourdon tube, is connected to the steam at the top of the boiler. As pressure rises the tube tries to straighten, and a little gear turns that movement into the needle's swing. Because steam pressure and temperature go together, the gauge is really telling you how hot the boiler is.
keyNumbers: 1.2 bar in the boiler means about 123 °C
Some machines add a second gauge for brew pressure, reading about 9 bar
details.madeOf: A brass Bourdon tube and gears in a chrome-plated case with a glass front.

parts.name: Boiler pressure gauge

parts.description: Rocker switch that turns the machine on; it then needs 20 minutes or so for the heavy group to warm through.

details.didYouKnow: Plenty of owners plug their machine into a timer socket so it switches itself on half an hour before they wake up.
details.howItWorks: Switching on lets the pressurestat power the heating element. The boiler builds pressure in about 10 to 15 minutes, but the heavy brass group heats only through the thermosiphon loop and takes longer, so most people leave it 20 to 30 minutes before the first shot.
keyNumbers: Group fully warm in about 20 to 30 minutes
details.madeOf: A rocker switch in a plastic body, rated for the full mains current of the element, often with a built-in lamp.

parts.name: Power switch

parts.description: Second dial showing the pressure the pump is pushing through the coffee, about 9 bar during a shot.

details.didYouKnow: Baristas sometimes fit a blank basket with no holes and run the pump against it: with nowhere for the water to go, the gauge shows the pressure the bypass valve is set to, which is how that valve is adjusted.
details.howItWorks: This second gauge reads the pressure of the water being pushed into the coffee, tapped from the line between the pump and the group. During a shot it usually settles at around 9 bar; the pump can make more, so a valve bleeds the excess back to the reservoir. Read beside the boiler gauge, it shows the two very different pressures in the machine: a gentle push of steam, and the hard shove of the pump.
keyNumbers: Around 9 bar during a typical shot
Reads higher against a blank basket, since nothing can flow
details.madeOf: A Bourdon-tube gauge like the boiler one, in a chrome bezel, connected by a thin copper or steel capillary. The narrow tube damps the pump's pulses so the needle doesn't shake too much.

parts.name: Brew pressure gauge

parts.description: Knob that opens the steam valve, letting steam from the top of the boiler out of the steam wand.

details.didYouKnow: Some newer machines use a lever instead of a knob for the steam, so it can be snapped fully on and off with one hand while you hold the milk jug.
details.howItWorks: Turning the knob unscrews a valve on the steam pipe from the top of the boiler. Steam at over 100 °C rushes out through the wand, and the further you open it, the faster it flows. Close it and a seal shuts the flow off again.
keyNumbers: Releases steam at about 1 to 1.5 bar
A couple of turns from shut to fully open
details.madeOf: A heat-resistant plastic knob on a brass or stainless spindle, closing against a rubber or PTFE seal.

parts.name: Steam knob

parts.description: Knob that opens a valve to draw hot water straight from the boiler, for tea or an Americano.

details.didYouKnow: Drawing lots of hot water at once can drop the boiler temperature, so it's usually better to make an Americano's water first and the shot second.
details.howItWorks: This valve is connected low down in the boiler, below the water line. Opening it lets the boiler's own pressure push hot water out through the wand. The autofill then tops the boiler back up with cold water.
keyNumbers: Usually limited to a cup or two at a time
details.madeOf: Plastic knob on a brass valve with a rubber or PTFE seal.

parts.name: Hot water knob

parts.description: Swivelling steel tube with a small holed tip that blasts steam into milk to heat and froth it.

details.didYouKnow: Milk proteins form the foam and milk fat makes it taste rich, which is why whole milk is easiest to steam and why most barista-style plant milks have added proteins.
details.howItWorks: Steam blasts out of small holes in the tip, just below the surface of the milk. That draws in air to make foam and stirs the jug into a whirlpool, so the bubbles get broken into a fine, glossy microfoam. Once the jug is too hot to hold, at around 60 to 65 °C, the milk is done.
keyNumbers: Steams a jug for a latte in about 30 to 60 seconds
details.madeOf: Stainless steel tube on a ball joint so it can swing, with a screw-on tip that has two to four holes.

parts.name: Steam wand

parts.description: Shorter spout on the other side that delivers hot water from the boiler.

details.didYouKnow: Adding hot water to espresso was popularised, the story goes, by American soldiers in Italy who wanted something closer to the coffee they knew at home.
details.howItWorks: A short spout that delivers hot water from the boiler. It's handy for warming cups, rinsing, making tea or topping up an espresso into an Americano.
keyNumbers: A cup in a few seconds
details.madeOf: Stainless steel tube with a plain open end.

parts.name: Hot water wand

parts.description: Heavy chrome-plated brass block that holds the portafilter, with valves inside worked by the lever on top.

details.didYouKnow: The E61 was named after the 1961 solar eclipse; it was one of the first machines to use an electric pump rather than a spring-loaded lever, and its design is still copied by dozens of makers.
details.howItWorks: The group is where the coffee is made. When you lift the lever, a cam inside opens valves that let hot water from the heat exchanger flow down through the group, first gently to soak the coffee and then at full pump pressure. Hot water circulating through it from the thermosiphon keeps its heavy brass body at a steady temperature, so each shot is brewed at much the same heat as the last.
details.madeOf: A casting of brass, about 4 kg of it, plated with chrome, with springs, seals and a small cam inside.

parts.name: E61 group head

parts.description: Lever on top of the group: lifted, it starts the pump and opens the brew valve; lowered, it stops and vents.

details.didYouKnow: A spring-loaded chamber in the group fills before full pressure reaches the coffee, giving a few seconds of gentle soaking known as pre-infusion.
details.howItWorks: Lifting the lever turns a cam inside the group, which opens the inlet valve and presses a micro-switch that starts the pump. Lowering it shuts the inlet and opens a third, drain path, so the pressure left above the coffee puck escapes into the drip tray instead of spraying when you remove the portafilter.
keyNumbers: Starts the pump through a micro-switch
details.madeOf: Chrome-plated brass arm, often with a plastic or wooden ball on the end.

parts.name: Brew lever

parts.description: Rubber ring inside the bottom of the group that the basket's rim presses against to seal in the pressure.

details.didYouKnow: When a gasket gets old and hard you have to twist the portafilter further and further round to stop it leaking, which is the clue it's time for a new one.
details.howItWorks: The portafilter's basket rim presses up into this rubber ring as you twist it in. The tighter fit seals in about 9 bar of pressure, so all the water has to go through the coffee instead of round it.
details.madeOf: Heat-resistant rubber or silicone, moulded into a thick ring.

parts.name: Group gasket

parts.description: Fine steel mesh that spreads the water evenly over the coffee instead of letting it hit in one jet.

details.didYouKnow: Rancid coffee oils on a dirty shower screen can make good beans taste bitter, which is why baristas backflush the group with detergent regularly.
details.howItWorks: Water arrives in the group through just a few holes. The screen breaks that into a fine shower spread evenly over the whole coffee puck, so no spot gets blasted and dug out while another stays dry.
keyNumbers: Should be scrubbed or swapped when coffee oils build up
details.madeOf: A fine stainless-steel mesh, sometimes on a perforated backing plate.

parts.name: Shower screen

parts.description: Chrome-plated brass holder that twists into the group on two lugs, with spouts underneath to pour into the cup.

details.didYouKnow: Many baristas keep the portafilter locked in the group between shots, because a cold portafilter would chill the next shot.
details.howItWorks: The portafilter holds the basket of coffee and locks into the group with two lugs on its rim that slide into slots and tighten with a quarter turn. Coffee flows from the basket through a channel in its base and out of the spouts underneath, usually split into two so it can fill two cups.
keyNumbers: Locks in with a quarter turn
details.madeOf: Chrome-plated brass, which is heavy, holds heat well and resists corrosion, with stainless-steel spouts.

parts.name: Portafilter

parts.description: Heat-proof handle used to lock the portafilter in with a firm quarter turn.

details.didYouKnow: Swapping the handle for a wooden one is one of the most popular small upgrades among home espresso enthusiasts.
details.howItWorks: The handle gives you the leverage to lock the portafilter firmly into the group and to knock out the used puck. It stays cool enough to hold while the brass end is almost as hot as the group.
keyNumbers: Takes the full twist to lock in
details.madeOf: Heat-resistant plastic such as phenolic resin, or wood on fancier machines, around a steel rod screwed into the portafilter.

parts.name: Portafilter handle

parts.description: Thin steel cup with hundreds of tiny holes in its floor that holds the packed coffee and lets the espresso out.

details.didYouKnow: The grind is the main thing a barista adjusts: too coarse and the water rushes through in 10 seconds, too fine and it drips out after a minute.
details.howItWorks: About 18 g of finely ground coffee is levelled and pressed hard into the basket, called tamping. Water pushed through the puck dissolves oils and flavour, and the many tiny holes in the floor let the liquid espresso out while holding back the grounds. The puck's resistance is what lets the pump build up 9 bar.
keyNumbers: Holds about 18 g for a double shot
Hundreds of holes, each a fraction of a millimetre
Yields about 36 g of espresso in 25 to 30 seconds
details.madeOf: Thin stamped stainless steel, with hundreds of precisely punched holes.

parts.name: Filter basket

parts.description: Clear plastic tank in the back that holds the water; it lifts out to fill at the tap.

details.didYouKnow: Very hard tap water slowly lines the boiler and pipes with limescale, so many owners use filtered or bottled water with just enough minerals for flavour.
details.howItWorks: The reservoir is simply a tank of cold water. The pump sucks from a hose that dips into the bottom, and a float or a sensor warns you when it's nearly empty so the pump doesn't run dry. Lifting it out to fill at the tap is easier than pouring in from a jug.
keyNumbers: Enough for about 30 to 50 shots and some steaming
Lifts out of the top or back
details.madeOf: Clear food-safe plastic so you can see how full it is.

parts.name: Water reservoir

parts.description: Soft silicone hose that the pump sucks water up through from the bottom of the reservoir.

details.didYouKnow: If the hose end lifts out of the water the pump sucks air and suddenly gets very loud, the first sign the tank is empty on machines without a sensor.
details.howItWorks: The hose runs from the bottom of the reservoir to the pump's inlet. The pump sucks water up through it, often past a small filter on the end that stops bits getting in.
keyNumbers: Carries cold water at normal pressure
Often has a small mesh filter on the end
details.madeOf: Soft food-grade silicone tubing, which stays flexible and doesn't taint the water.

parts.name: Intake hose

parts.description: Small pump in which an electromagnet shakes a piston back and forth 50 times a second, pushing water to about 15 bar.

details.didYouKnow: Vibration pumps are cheap and tiny but buzzy; bigger home machines often use a rotary pump instead, the quiet sort found in café machines.
details.howItWorks: Inside, an electromagnet is switched on and off by the mains 50 times a second, pulling a small piston one way while a spring pushes it back. Each stroke shoves a tiny squirt of water past a one-way valve, building pressure. An over-pressure valve after it lets the excess back to the tank, so the coffee sees about 9 bar instead of the pump's full 15.
keyNumbers: Strokes 50 times a second on UK mains
details.madeOf: A plastic and brass body around a copper coil, with a steel piston, a spring and a rubber one-way valve.

parts.name: Vibration pump

parts.description: Pipe that carries water under pressure from the pump to the valve block.

details.didYouKnow: Copper is used for most espresso plumbing because it's easy to bend, joins well and passes heat readily.
details.howItWorks: This pipe carries the pump's output under full pressure to the valve block, where it splits: one path goes through the solenoid to refill the boiler, and the other goes to the heat-exchanger tube to become brewing water.
keyNumbers: Cold water on its way in
details.madeOf: Copper or braided stainless steel hose with crimped brass fittings.

parts.name: Pump outlet pipe

parts.description: Electrically opened valve that lets the pump top up the boiler when a probe senses the water level has dropped.

details.didYouKnow: That short burst of pump noise you hear after steaming milk is the autofill: the solenoid opening to replace the water you turned into steam.
details.howItWorks: The valve is opened by an electromagnet. A probe in the boiler measures the water level by whether the water touches it and completes a tiny electric circuit. When the level drops, the controller opens the solenoid and runs the pump until the water reaches the probe again.
keyNumbers: Opens in a fraction of a second
Tops up a few tens of millilitres at a time
details.madeOf: A brass valve body with a rubber seal, and a copper coil sealed in black plastic.

parts.name: Autofill solenoid valve

parts.description: Pipe from the solenoid valve up into the bottom of the boiler, carrying fresh water to refill it.

details.didYouKnow: A non-return valve stops boiling water from the boiler being pushed back towards the pump when it's not running.
details.howItWorks: This pipe carries cold water from the solenoid valve up into the boiler. It usually enters low down so the new cold water mixes into the hot water rather than collapsing the steam on top.
keyNumbers: Opens only when the autofill runs
details.madeOf: Copper tube with brass compression fittings.

parts.name: Boiler fill pipe

parts.description: Pipe from the valve block into the front of the boiler, feeding cold water into the heat-exchanger tube when you brew.

details.didYouKnow: Changing the injector's hole size is a classic way to make an E61 machine brew a little hotter or cooler.
details.howItWorks: When you lift the brew lever, the pump pushes cold water up this pipe into the heat-exchanger tube in the boiler. Usually it enters through a little nozzle called an injector, which helps keep the thermosiphon circulating in the right direction.
keyNumbers: Carries water at about 9 bar when brewing
Enters the front of the boiler
details.madeOf: Copper tube with brass fittings.

parts.name: Heat-exchanger feed pipe

parts.description: Insulated copper tank, about 1.8 litres, kept about two-thirds full of water with steam on top at around 1.2 bar.

details.didYouKnow: Because water boils at a higher temperature under pressure, a pressurised boiler can hold water hotter than 100 °C without boiling it away; a pressure cooker works the same way.
details.howItWorks: The boiler is kept about two-thirds full of water and heated well above boiling point. It's sealed, so the steam on top builds up pressure, and at about 1.2 bar the water stays liquid at around 123 °C. That's too hot for coffee but perfect for steam, and it's the heat source the heat-exchanger tube draws on for brewing water.
keyNumbers: Safety valve opens at about 2 bar
details.madeOf: Copper, often nickel-plated inside to resist scale, with brass end plates, and a safety valve on top. It's usually wrapped in insulation.

parts.name: Boiler

parts.description: Looped electric element in the bottom of the boiler, typically about 1,200 to 1,400 watts.

details.didYouKnow: If the boiler ever ran dry, the element would overheat in seconds, so there's also a thermal fuse on the boiler that cuts the power if it gets far too hot.
details.howItWorks: A coiled wire inside a sealed steel tube heats up when current flows through it, like a kettle element bent into a loop. It sits under the water at the bottom of the boiler, so all its heat goes straight into the water.
keyNumbers: Heats the boiler in about 10 to 15 minutes
Switched on and off by the pressurestat
details.madeOf: Nickel-chrome resistance wire packed in magnesium oxide powder, which conducts heat but not electricity, inside a stainless-steel or copper sheath.

parts.name: Heating element

parts.description: Copper tube running through the boiler; brewing water passes through it and is heated by the hotter water around it.

details.didYouKnow: Water left still in the tube overheats, so after the machine sits idle owners do a 'cooling flush', running the group for a few seconds until the hissing stops.
details.howItWorks: The heat-exchanger tube runs through the boiler, surrounded by water at about 123 °C. Fresh water passing through it picks up heat without ever mixing with the boiler water, and comes out at about 90 to 96 °C on its way to the group. That way the machine can steam milk and brew coffee at the same time with just one boiler.
keyNumbers: Holds a couple of hundred millilitres
details.madeOf: Copper tube, chosen because it passes heat very quickly.

parts.name: Heat-exchanger tube

parts.description: Upper pipe of the loop between the heat exchanger and the group; hot water rises through one pipe and sinks back through the other.

details.didYouKnow: Some owners fit a small restrictor in the thermosiphon to slow the flow and cool an E61 group that runs too hot.
details.howItWorks: Hot water is lighter than cooler water, so it rises. Water warmed in the heat exchanger rises up one pipe into the group, gives up some heat to the brass and sinks back through the other pipe as it cools. The loop circulates on its own with no pump, keeping the group hot all the time.
keyNumbers: Flows with no pump at all
Keeps the group at about 90 to 95 °C
details.madeOf: Copper pipe with brass fittings at each end.

parts.name: Thermosiphon upper pipe

parts.description: Lower pipe of the loop, joining the bottom of the heat exchanger to the group head.

details.didYouKnow: The same thermosiphon effect once heated whole houses: old hot-water radiator systems circulated the same way, with no pump at all.
details.howItWorks: This is the other half of the loop. It joins the bottom of the heat exchanger to the group, so water can circulate round the loop and through the group without a pump.
keyNumbers: Part of a loop that circulates all day
Joined to the group behind the front panel
details.madeOf: Copper pipe with brass fittings.

parts.name: Thermosiphon lower pipe

parts.description: Pressure switch that turns the element on and off to hold the boiler at its set pressure, and so its temperature.

details.didYouKnow: Many newer machines swap the pressurestat for an electronic temperature controller called a PID, which holds the boiler within a degree or so instead of swinging up and down.
details.howItWorks: Steam pressure from the boiler pushes on a flexible diaphragm inside. When the pressure reaches its setting, the diaphragm snaps a pair of contacts open and switches the element off; as the pressure falls, it snaps them closed again. A screw sets the pressure, which in turn sets the temperature of the whole machine.
keyNumbers: Switches the full current of the element
Swings up and down by about 0.2 bar
details.madeOf: A brass diaphragm chamber and silver electrical contacts in a plastic housing.

parts.name: Pressurestat

summary: A home E61-style espresso machine: a vibration pump pushes water from a reservoir into a copper boiler, and a heavy chrome group head forces it at about 9 bar through finely ground coffee packed in a portafilter.
